2.text: “It was in the Chukochya (adjective from Chukchee) hamlet. This hamlet lies forty miles to

3.text: the west of Pokhotsk. It is now uninhabited, save that some fishing is done there early in the

4.text: fall. There was a watch-tower there. Now it has fallen down, and lies on its side. It happened

5.text: long ago. The tower was built to watch from there for the Chukchee. It was quite large. Every

6.text: wall was four sashen (twenty-eight feet) high. Its top was on exactly the same level as the church

7.text: in the town (of Nishne-Kolymsk). It had two floors, one below and another above. One time an

8.text: old man stood on the top of the tower watching. The morning was dawning. He looked over

9.text: the river (a tributary of the Kolyma, the so-called ‘Chukchee Channel,’ quite narrow and quiet).

10.text: The trunk of a tree, lying on its side, was visible, and all at once it appeared to him as if a man

11.text: clad in a Chukchee overcoat, — an overcoat made of seal-intestines, similar to our window-covering, —

12.text: were stepping over that trunk. The old man said to the younger people, ‘Look here, boys! It

13.text: seems as if the Chukchee were stealing about and wanted to attack our village.’ The younger

14.text: people did not believe him. He took a bag on his back, a walking-staff in his hand, and walked

15.text: away to Pokhotsk. They staid there for the summer, then for the fall also. When the nights

16.text: grew longer, the Chukchee came, surprised them in their sleep, and killed all of them. As soon

17.text: as any one ran out of the house, they would kill him then and there. Two brothers, however,

18.text: were so nimble that the Chuckchee could not, in spite of all their efforts, either stab them with

19.text: spears, or hit them with arrows. So they ran about. At last the older brother passed by an old

20.text: Chukchee woman sitting on a reindeer-sledge, — so old she could hardly walk. She threw a bone

21.text: arrow at him and hit him under the knee. He fell down, and exclaimed, ‘Oh, you, my brother!

22.text: Do you want to live in the world all alone by yourself? How could you live like that?’ The

23.text: other immediately surrendered, and both were killed. Still another young man fell down among

24.text: the dead with face upwards, simulating death. He lay there thus, and looked on. They dressed

25.text: one brother in an overcoat of white reindeer-skins, and on the other one they put an overcoat of

26.text: spotted reindeer-skins. They laid the first one on bedding of white skin, and the other on bedding

27.text: of spotted skin. The old woman, unable to walk, crept along from corpse to corpse, and looked

28.text: into each face. When she reached the one feigning death, she took her tailoring-knife. It was

29.text: of iron and very old, with no edge, because the Chukchee in that time had hardly any iron. With

30.text: that blunt-edged knife she began to chop him quite slowly across the forehead. Tap, tap! tap, tap!

31.text: She broke all the middle portion of his forehead; but he uttered not a sound, God granted him

32.text: such patience. When they had gone, he arose and went to Pokhotsk with the news. The

33.text: report was sent to the fortress of Nishne-Kolymsk. At that time the Cossacks in the fortress were

34.text: as numerous as mosquitoes. The magazines, at present empty, were filled with flour up to the

35.text: ceiling. So a party was sent, properly armed, to overtake the Chukchee. They came to the

36.text: Chukochya hamlet, and saw smoke off the ridge of hills, — the so-called ‘Chukchee Ridge,’ to the

37.text: west of the Kolyma. Still they did not want to have a fight. In those days they were afraid of

38.text: the very name of the Chukchee. So they played false, and said nothing about the smoke. They

39.text: came back and said, ‘We have seen nothing.’

40.text: “In after times the Chukchee related the following: ‘We came from over the river upon the

41.text: ice, and spent the summer on the Chukchee Ridge. When the Russians came to hunt moulting

42.text: geese, we tried to throw our grass insoles¹ across the path of those who were friendly to us, in

43.text: order to make them think of it; but they paid no attention.’ After that the Chukchee wandered

44.text: in various directions. One party reached the Indighirka River. Some young men went to hunt

45.text: geese. There was an old man, Portniaghin, on the Portniaghin fishing-coast. They came to him,

46.text: and said, ‘It is very strange! When we are hunting geese, Chukchee bone arrows come over to

47.text: us from somewhere. One of our number has already been killed. Still, when we land on the

48.text: shore and look for the enemy, we are unable to find anything.’ He said, ‘Take me to that

49.text: place. Perhaps I can find them.’ So they went together. ‘Where is the place?’ — ‘This

50.text: here.’ They landed, and ascended the bank, but nobody was there. Only a number of

51.text: hummocks were to be seen on the swampy plain, — very many of them, and quite big ones.

52.text: ‘There!’ said the old man, ‘shoot at those hummocks!’ They shot at the hummocks. With every

53.text: ¹ The grass insoles of the Chukchee boot are more obtuse and rounder at the toe than those of the

54.text: Russians. An experienced eye can distinguish without much trouble one from the other (compare p. 239).
